newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians face shortages over Greek dispute.
newsitem.headline: Albanians face shortages over Greek dispute.

text.p: Albanians are faced with the prospect of empty shops over Christmas and New Year because of the Greek farmers' blockade.

Customs officials said around 150 trucks left Albania for Greece on Thursday, hoping to use country routes to get around main roads which have been blocked for 22 days with tractors, causing transport chaos and inflicting $100 million of damage on the Greek economy.

The Greek blockade is pinching the economy of Albania, Europe's poorest country, forcing several factories to shut down and causing price hikes of up to 20 percent in the main southern town of Gjirokaster.
Greece is Albania's second most important trading partner, accounting for some 20 percent of all imports.

Truck drivers said they had taken the arrival in Albania of six buses with Albanians and ethnic Greek immigrant workers and 15 trucks from Greece earlier in the week as a signal that it was possible to make the journey.

The drivers said they hoped to return from Greece with wine, beer and other alcoholic drinks that have become a scarce commodity in Albania as well as oranges, apples and potatoes, the price of which had gone up by a record 30 percent.
"Our patience has run out, we can't wait any longer. Our market needs the goods so badly," Altin Doko, a trader on Gjirokaster's main market, told Reuters.
Items such as pastry layers, widely used to make sweets which are part of Albania's traditional New Year's fare, toys and Christmas tree lights have all but disappeared from shop shelves.
A plastic Christmas tree now costs 2,500 leks ($24), almost 80 percent more than last year. And unless trucks can bring some electric tree lights back, the trees will have to remain bare.
A small croissant factory, the only one in the country, has stopped production because it has not received any raw materials from Greece for 10 days.

The region's biggest company, Greek-Albanian joint venture Recor Albania which produces shoes and processes leather, was forced to halt most of its production lines for the first time in its 70-year history, managers said.
"We process Albanian hides but we import our chemicals from abroad," said deputy director Thoma Muzina, adding there was a stock of 42,000 pairs of finished shoes the company was unable to export.
Muzina said the factory would have to close down next week unless the situation changed.
